question: Let $A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & a & -1 \\ -a & 0 & b \\ 1 & -b & 0 \end{bmatrix}$ where $a, b$ are real numbers. If $A$ is skew symmetric, prove that $a$ and $b$ can be any real numbers and further show $|A|=0$.
explanation:
By definition, a matrix $A$ is skew symmetric if $A' = -A$.
First check if $A$ is skew symmetric.
$A' = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -a & 1 \\ a & 0 & -b \\ -1 & b & 0 \end{bmatrix}$
$-A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -a & 1 \\ a & 0 & -b \\ -1 & b & 0 \end{bmatrix}$
Thus, $A' = -A$ for any $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$.
Now calculate $|A|$.
Expanding using first row:
$|A| = 0 - a((-a)*0 - 1*b) + (-1)((-a)(-b) - 1*0)$
$= -a(-b) -(-1)(ab)$
$= ab - ab$
$= 0$
Thus $|A|=0$ for all $a, b$.

options.A: $A$ is skew symmetric only when $a=0$ and $b=0$, and $|A|=1$.
options.B: $A'=-A$ for all real $a,b$, so $a$ and $b$ can be any real numbers; also, since $A$ is a $3\times3$ skew symmetric matrix, $|A|=0$.
options.C: $A$ is symmetric for all real $a,b$, so $|A|=ab$.
options.D: $A$ is skew symmetric only when $a=b$, and $|A|=a^2+b^2$.
